chapter.title: Stations and the belt

cards.body:
Chapter 1 rang the bell. Now watch what moves. Every box on the n8n canvas is a *node*: one station on the line, with one job. What slides along the belt between stations is an *item*: a small tray of named fields, like name: Priya, order: 2 lattes.

**Each station takes the tray, does its one job, and slides it on.** Lift the lid at any station and you can see exactly what is on the tray as it leaves.
cards.simpler: Chapter 1 showed how a workflow starts. Now look at what moves. Every box on the n8n canvas is a node. Think of it as one station on a factory line with one job. The thing that slides between stations is an item: a small tray of named fields, like name: Priya, order: 2 lattes. **Each station takes the tray, does its one job, and slides it on.** Lift the lid at any station and you see exactly what is on the tray as it leaves.

cards.prompt: Station 2 is supposed to stamp a date on Priya's tray. Station 3 says no date ever arrived. Where do you look to find out what station 2 actually put on the tray?

options.text: Read station 2's instruction card, the settings you typed in
Lift the lid at station 2 and look at the tray leaving it
Ask station 1, since it handled the tray first

whyNot.a: That's what the station was told to do, not what it did: a card can read fine while the tray leaves without a stamp.
whyNot.c: That's upstream: station 1 only knows what it handed over. The belt moves one way, and the question is what left station 2.

cards.reteach: A station's settings are a promise. The tray leaving it is the truth. When something is missing downstream, look at what actually left the station you suspect, not at what you asked it to do.

cards.title: One box, one job
cards.body:
On the canvas, click the small plus on a node's right edge to add the next node. The line that appears is the belt. **A node does one job**: it gets data, changes data, or sends data somewhere. If you want two things done, you add two nodes.

An *item* is what travels. It is a packet of named fields, written in *JSON*, a text format that lists name and value pairs inside curly braces. A run may carry 1 item or 40. Most nodes do their job once per item, so 40 trays in means 40 jobs done.
cards.simpler: On the canvas, click the small plus on the right edge of a node to add the next one. The line that appears is the belt. **A node does one job**: it gets data, changes data, or sends data somewhere. Want two things done? Add two nodes. An item is what travels. It is a packet of named fields written in JSON, a text format that lists names and values inside curly braces. A run may carry 1 item or 40. Most nodes do their job once per item, so 40 trays in means 40 jobs done.

cards.title: Rosa's three empty stations
cards.body: Rosa builds three nodes with no apps attached: a Manual Trigger, then an Edit Fields node that sets name to Rosa and drink to flat white, then a second Edit Fields that adds size: large, with *Include Other Input Fields* switched on so the first two ride along. She clicks Test workflow. The trigger shows 1 item with almost nothing in it. Node 2 shows 1 item with 2 fields. Node 3 shows 1 item with 3 fields. Without that switch, node 3 would have handed on a tray carrying only size, and Rosa would be ordering a large nothing.
cards.simpler: Rosa builds three nodes with no apps attached. First a Manual Trigger. Then an Edit Fields node that sets name to Rosa and drink to flat white. Then a second Edit Fields that adds size: large, with Include Other Input Fields switched on so the first two fields ride along. She clicks Test workflow. The trigger shows 1 item with almost nothing in it. Node 2 shows 1 item with 2 fields. Node 3 shows 1 item with 3 fields. Without that switch, node 3 would hand on a tray carrying only size. Rosa would be ordering a large nothing.

cards.prompt: Dev's workflow has three nodes. The third builds a greeting and comes out as 'Hello, undefined'. He wants to know what node 2 really handed over. What does he click?

options.text: Node 2, then reads its output panel on the right in JSON view
Node 3's settings, and retypes the greeting more carefully
The trigger, to run the whole thing again and hope

whyNot.b: That's the station's instruction card, not the tray: the greeting can be typed perfectly while the field it asks for never arrived.
whyNot.c: That's the bell: it starts the run, but only node 2's output panel shows what node 2 passed on.

cards.reteach: Undefined means node 3 reached for a field that was not on the tray. The tray came from node 2, so node 2's output is where the answer lives. Open it and read the field names as they are actually spelled.

cards.title: Reading the panel
cards.body:
Click any node after a run. The panel opens with what came in on the left and **what went out on the right**. The output has three views: Table for a glance, JSON for the exact spelling of every field name, Schema for a plain list of names.

The top of the panel says how many items: 1 item, 12 items. If the count drops between two nodes, that node dropped trays.

Before a run the panels are empty. Press *Test step* on one node to run just that station, using the previous node's last output. You do not need to ring the bell every time.
cards.simpler: After a run, click any node. A panel opens. What came in is on the left. **What went out is on the right.** The output has three views. Table gives a quick glance. JSON shows the exact spelling of every field name. Schema gives a plain list of names. The top of the panel says how many items, like 1 item or 12 items. If the count drops between two nodes, that node dropped trays. Before a run the panels are empty. Press Test step on one node to run just that station, using the previous node's last output. You do not need to start the whole workflow every time.

cards.body: Marcus's second node creates a field called Customer Name, with a space. His third node asks for customerName. It comes back blank, and he spends 20 minutes re-reading node 3's settings. **The fix was one click away**: open node 2's output in JSON view and read the name letter by letter. Spelling, spaces and capitals must match exactly, or the next station is reaching for a tray that does not exist.
cards.simpler: Marcus's second node creates a field called Customer Name, with a space. His third node asks for customerName. It comes back blank. He spends 20 minutes re-reading the settings of node 3. **The fix was one click away**: open the output of node 2 in JSON view and read the name letter by letter. Spelling, spaces and capitals must match exactly. If they do not, the next station reaches for a tray that does not exist.

cards.prompt: After a run, node 2's output panel says 12 items. Node 3 is a node that adds a field. How many times does node 3 do its job?

options.text: Depends how long you leave it running

whyNot.a: That's the workflow run, which happens once: inside it, a node works tray by tray, and 12 trays arrived.
whyNot.c: That's thinking of it like a machine with a speed dial: a node does its job exactly once per item that arrives, no more, no less.

cards.reteach: Items are trays. A node is a station that handles each tray that reaches it. 12 trays in means the station does its one job 12 times and, unless it drops some, 12 trays go out.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every box is a node that does one job on each item, a packet of named fields, then hands it to the next box. **After a run, click a node and its output panel shows exactly what it passed on**, every field name spelled as it really is.
cards.simpler: Every box is a node. It does one job on each item, which is a packet of named fields. Then it hands the item to the next box. **After a run, click a node and its output panel shows exactly what it passed on.** Every field name appears spelled as it really is. This is like checking a tray at the end of a station before it moves down the line.

cards.body: Open yesterday's workflow. Add an Edit Fields node after the trigger and set one field, name, to your name. Click Test workflow, then open that node and read its output in JSON view. Count the items.
cards.simpler: Open the workflow you built yesterday. Add an Edit Fields node right after the trigger. Set one field, called name, to your own name. Click Test workflow. Then open that node and read its output in JSON view. Count how many items it shows. This is the same lid-lifting check from earlier, done on your own line.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now connect three nodes in a row and read exactly what each station hands to the next.
